claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted cancer care, raising concerns regarding the impact of wait time, or 'lag time', on clinical outcomes.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted cancer care, raising concerns regarding the impact of wait time, or 'lag time', on clinical outcomes.
evidence: This is a general statement about the pandemic's impact on cancer care, drawing from established knowledge about COVID-19's effects on healthcare systems.

claim: By May 2020, two months after the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak a pandemic, the volume of colorectal and breast cancer screenings in the United States dropped by 85% and 94%, respectively, compared to averages from the previous three years.
source: By May 2020, two months after the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak a pandemic, the volume of colorectal and breast cancer screenings in the United States dropped by 85% and 94%, respectively, compared to averages from the previous three years (Mast and Munoz del, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mast and Munoz del, 2020, providing specific data on screening volume reductions.

claim: Cancer screening services were temporarily suspended in the early months of the pandemic.
source: In the early months of the pandemic, cancer screening services were temporarily suspended (Mast and Munoz del, 2020; Maringe et al., 2020; Villain et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the suspension of screening services.

claim: For cancers that were diagnosed in the first six months of the pandemic, an increasing trend in diagnosis of late-stage cancers and a decreasing trend in diagnosis of early-stage cancers were observed.
source: For cancers that were diagnosed in the first six months of the pandemic, an increasing trend in diagnosis of late-stage cancers and a decreasing trend in diagnosis of early-stage cancers were observed, as a reflection of the initial effects of extended lag times to diagnosis (Carvalho et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carvalho et al., 2022, which provides observational data on cancer stage at diagnosis during the pandemic.

claim: The scoping review identified 9032 records through database searches.
source: We identified 9032 records through database searches, of which 29 were eligible.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1, which shows the PRISMA flow diagram with the number of records identified.

claim: The scoping review included 29 eligible records.
source: We identified 9032 records through database searches, of which 29 were eligible.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and confirmed by Figure 1, which shows 29 records included in the final analysis.

claim: The review classified 33 unique types of lag time intervals across 10 cancer sites.
source: We classified 33 unique types of lag time intervals across 10 cancer sites, of which breast, colorectal, head and neck, and ovarian cancers were investigated most.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2, which visually represents 33 lag time intervals (T1-T33).

claim: Breast, colorectal, head and neck, and ovarian cancers were investigated most frequently in the included reviews.
source: We classified 33 unique types of lag time intervals across 10 cancer sites, of which breast, colorectal, head and neck, and ovarian cancers were investigated most.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results section based on the analysis of included reviews.

claim: Two systematic reviews investigating lag time to diagnosis reported different findings regarding survival outcomes among paediatric patients with Ewing's sarcomas or central nervous system tumours.
source: Two systematic reviews investigating lag time to diagnosis reported different findings regarding survival outcomes among paediatric patients with Ewing's sarcomas or central nervous system tumours.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by detailed findings in Table 2 comparing Brasme et al., 2012 and Lethaby et al., 2013.

claim: Comparable risk estimates of mortality were found for lag time intervals from surgery to adjuvant chemotherapy for breast, colorectal, and ovarian cancers.
source: Comparable risk estimates of mortality were found for lag time intervals from surgery to adjuvant chemotherapy for breast, colorectal, and ovarian cancers.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by detailed risk estimates presented in Table 4.

claim: Risk estimates of pathologic complete response indicated an optimal time window of 7–8 weeks for neoadjuvant chemotherapy completion prior to surgery for rectal cancers.
source: Risk estimates of pathologic complete response indicated an optimal time window of 7–8 weeks for neoadjuvant chemotherapy completion prior to surgery for rectal cancers.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by detailed findings in Table 3 from multiple meta-analyses (Wang et al., 2016; Petrelli et al., 2016; Du et al., 2018).

claim: The review identified critical variations in lag time research design when comparing methods across meta-analyses on the same cancer sites, lag times, and outcomes.
source: In comparing methods across meta-analyses on the same cancer sites, lag times, and outcomes, we identified critical variations in lag time research design.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and elaborated in the Discussion section with specific examples of methodological variations.

claim: Four of 10 included studies reported no association between T33 and OS among patients who experienced T33 >45 days compared to those who experienced T33 <45 days in brain cancer patients.

evidence: This claim is stated in the meta-analysis findings section and is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2016.

claim: One meta-analysis found a significantly greater risk of mortality per 1-week increase in T32 (HR: 1.04, 95% CI [1.00–1.09]) among patients with ovarian cancer.
source: Of the two meta-analyses that evaluated the association between time from surgery to ACT (T32) and mortality among patients with ovarian cancer, one found a significantly greater risk of mortality per 1-week increase in T32 (HR: 1.04, 95% CI [1.00–1.09]) or among those who experienced extended T32 (HR: 1.18, 95% CI [1.06–1.32]) (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the meta-analysis findings section and is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2017, with specific risk estimates provided.

claim: One meta-analysis found a significantly greater risk of mortality among those who experienced extended T32 (HR: 1.18, 95% CI [1.06–1.32]) among patients with ovarian cancer.
source: Of the two meta-analyses that evaluated the association between time from surgery to ACT (T32) and mortality among patients with ovarian cancer, one found a significantly greater risk of mortality per 1-week increase in T32 (HR: 1.04, 95% CI [1.00–1.09]) or among those who experienced extended T32 (HR: 1.18, 95% CI [1.06–1.32]) (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the meta-analysis findings section and is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2017, with specific risk estimates provided.

claim: One meta-analysis reported no association between extended T32 and odds of 3-year mortality among patients with ovarian cancer.
source: The other meta-analysis reported no association between extended T32 and odds of 3-year mortality (Usón et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the meta-analysis findings section and is supported by citation to Usón et al., 2017.

claim: Wang et al. conducted subgroup analyses based on different cut-offs of T29 (5, 6, 7, 8, 10, and 12 weeks) and found that performing surgery at 7 and 8 weeks yielded a significantly improved pCR rates compared to performing surgery earlier, at 5 or 6 weeks, or later, at 10 or 12 weeks.
source: Considering this uncertainty, Wang et al. conducted subgroup analyses based on different cut-offs of T29 (5, 6, 7, 8, 10, and 12 weeks) (Supplementary file 3) and found that performing surgery at 7 and 8 weeks yielded a significantly improved pCR rates compared to performing surgery earlier, at 5 or 6 weeks, or later, at 10 or 12 weeks (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016, with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Surgery performed too soon may not allow for the maximal anti-tumourigenic response to NACRT among rectal cancer patients.
source: Among rectal cancer patients, surgery performed too soon may not allow for the maximal anti-tumourigenic response to NACRT, however, waiting too long could mitigate any potential benefit that could be maintained from NACRT and permit tumour repopulation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on inference from the data on optimal timing windows for surgery after NACRT.

claim: Waiting too long after NACRT could mitigate any potential benefit that could be maintained from NACRT and permit tumour repopulation among rectal cancer patients.
source: Among rectal cancer patients, surgery performed too soon may not allow for the maximal anti-tumourigenic response to NACRT, however, waiting too long could mitigate any potential benefit that could be maintained from NACRT and permit tumour repopulation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on inference from the data on optimal timing windows for surgery after NACRT.

claim: A UK population-based modelling study predicted increases of 7.9–9.6%, 15.3–16.6%, 4.8–5.3%, and 5.8–6.0% in deaths due to breast, colorectal, lung, and esophageal cancers, respectively, up to five years after diagnosis compared to pre-pandemic data.
source: A UK population-based modelling study predicting the impact of lag times to diagnosis of colorectal, breast, lung, and esophageal cancers on survival during the 12 months after national lockdown measures began estimated increases of 7.9–9.6%, 15.3–16.6%, 4.8–5.3%, and 5.8–6.0% in deaths due to breast, colorectal, lung, and esophageal cancers, respectively, up to five years after diagnosis compared to pre-pandemic data (Maringe et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citation to Maringe et al., 2020, which provides modelling predictions.

claim: A modelling study projected a 2% increase in cancer deaths, or an excess 355,172 life-years-lost, in Canada between 2020 and 2030 due to pandemic-induced lag times to both cancer diagnosis and treatment.
source: Another modelling study from our group projected a 2% increase in cancer deaths, or an excess 355,172 life-years-lost, in Canada between 2020 and 2030 due to pandemic-induced lag times to both cancer diagnosis and treatment, assuming the cancer care system returned to normal capacity in 2021 (Malagón et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citation to Malagón et al., 2022, which provides modelling predictions.

claim: The Aarhus statement identified unclear definitions of start and endpoints in lag times, as well as inconsistency in defining these points across studies evaluating the same lag time as primary obstacles to aggregating research on lag time to cancer diagnosis.
source: The Aarhus statement, a set of recommendations and checklist resulting from discussion regarding methodological concerns in research conducted on lag times to cancer diagnosis, identified unclear definitions of start and endpoints in lag times, as well as inconsistency in defining these points across studies evaluating the same lag time as primary obstacles to aggregating research on lag time to cancer diagnosis (Weller et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citation to Weller et al., 2012.

claim: Some of the included qualitative systematic reviews initially intended to meta-analyze the abstracted data, however, variability in start and endpoint definitions of lag times across included studies and in type of lag time variable prevented researchers from pursuing quantitative analyses.
source: Some of the included qualitative systematic reviews initially intended to meta-analyze the abstracted data (Hangaard Hansen et al., 2018; Graboyes et al., 2019; Foster et al., 2013; Lethaby et al., 2013), however, variability in start and endpoint definitions of lag times across included studies and in type of lag time variable (categorical vs. continuous) prevented researchers from pursuing quantitative analyses.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citations to multiple systematic reviews that encountered this methodological challenge.

claim: The waiting-time paradox is the implication that patients with more advanced-stage disease are prioritized for referral and subsequent treatment within a given health system more rapidly than patients with early-stage, less severe disease.
source: Otherwise monikered the 'waiting-time paradox', confounding by indication is the implication that patients with more advanced-stage disease are prioritized for referral and subsequent treatment within a given health system more rapidly than patients with early-stage, less severe disease.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and draws from established knowledge about confounding by indication in lag time research.

claim: The overall effect of the waiting-time paradox leads to the indication that early referral and/or treatment is associated with higher mortality.
source: The overall effect of this prioritization leads to the indication that early referral and/or treatment is associated with higher mortality; this survival trend is in direct contradiction with the typical log-linear approach taken in meta-analyses on the association between extended lag time to cancer treatment and risk of mortality.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and draws from established knowledge about the waiting-time paradox.

claim: The review searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library of Systematic Reviews for records published between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2019.
source: We systematically searched four electronic databases: MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library of Systematic Reviews. The search strategy consisted of the index keywords cancer, diagnosis & treatment, wait-time, delay, outcome, and systematic review and/or meta-analysis, along with their associated MeSH and iterative search terms (Supplementary file 1). We queried these databases for records published between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2019.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Methods section describing the search strategy.

claim: The review did not apply language restrictions in the search strategy.
source: We did not apply language restrictions.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Methods section describing the search strategy.

claim: A total of 20 meta-analyses and 9 systematic reviews were included in the current scoping review.
source: A total of 20 meta-analyses and 9 systematic reviews were included in the current scoping review.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Results section and confirmed by Figure 1.

claim: The present work was supported by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR-COVID-19 Rapid Research Funding opportunity, VR5-172666 grant to Eduardo L. Franco).
source: The present work was supported by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR-COVID-19 Rapid Research Funding opportunity, VR5-172666 grant to Eduardo L. Franco).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Funding section of the abstract.

claim: Parker Tope, Eliya Farah, and Rami Ali each received an MSc. stipend from the Gerald Bronfman Department of Oncology, McGill University.
source: Parker Tope, Eliya Farah, and Rami Ali each received an MSc. stipend from the Gerald Bronfman Department of Oncology, McGill University.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Funding section of the abstract.

claim: The Lyon R90-01 trial established 6–8 weeks as an accepted lag time of NART or NACRT after surgery in clinical practice for rectal cancer.
source: These cut-offs were determined based on the seminal Lyon R90-01 trial, which investigated the impact of 6–8 weeks between NART and sphincter-preserving surgery compared to 2 weeks on pathological downstaging among patients with rectal cancer and established 6–8 weeks as an accepted lag time of NART or NACRT after surgery in clinical practice (Francois et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citation to Francois et al., 1999.

claim: Biagi et al., 2011 excluded four studies that were included in Des Guetz et al.'s analysis based on lack of adjustment for potential confounders.
source: Biagi et al., 2011 excluded four studies (Berglund et al., 2008; André et al., 2007; Gray et al., 2007; Taal et al., 2001) that were included in Des Guetz et al.'s analysis (Raphael et al., 2016) based on lack of adjustment for potential confounders.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section comparing methodological differences between meta-analyses.

claim: The review's restriction on publication date of included systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses does not prevent the inclusion of studies that evaluate interventions that have since evolved in type, dosing, and/or timing.
source: Nevertheless, our restriction on publication date of included systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses does not prevent the inclusion of studies that evaluate interventions that have since evolved in type, dosing, and/or timing.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of the review methodology.

claim: Future ubiquity of novel therapies under the purview of precision medicine will necessitate consideration of the evolution of cancer care in meta-analytical lag time research.
source: Indeed, future ubiquity of novel therapies under the purview of precision medicine will necessitate consideration of the evolution of cancer care in meta-analytical lag time research.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on speculation about future research needs.

claim: Conducting sensitivity analyses based on treatment type, regimen, or date of publication can provide a clearer understanding of the external validity of reported risk estimates.
source: In such cases, conducting sensitivity analyses based on treatment type, regimen, or date of publication can provide a clearer understanding of the external validity of reported risk estimates.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a recommendation for future research.

claim: Refinements of the Aarhus statement integrating suggestions from clinicians and cancer diagnosis researchers have been proposed, yet are still restricted to cancer diagnosis, rather than applicable to the entire cancer care continuum.
source: Refinements of the Aarhus statement integrating suggestions from clinicians and cancer diagnosis researchers have been proposed (Coxon et al., 2018), yet are still restricted to cancer diagnosis, rather than applicable to the entire cancer care continuum.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citation to Coxon et al., 2018.

claim: Restricting the search to systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses published after 2010 did not prevent the introduction of medical interventions that have changed over time in included literature.
source: Restricting our search to systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses published after 2010 did not prevent the introduction of medical interventions that have changed over time in included literature, however, our reporting of stratified analyses performed in included meta-analyses, when available, by treatment specifications (e.g., dosing, chemotherapy type) does provide context regarding modification of lag time on clinical outcomes by intervention modality.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of the review.

claim: Differences in reporting across included systematic reviews and meta-analyses prevented the ability to provide aggregated summary statistics of the associations between lag time and oncologic outcomes.
source: Moreover, differences in reporting across included systematic reviews and meta-analyses prevented our ability to provide (1) aggregated summary statistics of the associations between lag time and oncologic outcomes, and (2) the distribution of lag times experienced by patients included in each study within each meta-analysis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of the review.

claim: Differences in reporting across included systematic reviews and meta-analyses prevented the ability to provide the distribution of lag times experienced by patients included in each study within each meta-analysis.
source: Moreover, differences in reporting across included systematic reviews and meta-analyses prevented our ability to provide (1) aggregated summary statistics of the associations between lag time and oncologic outcomes, and (2) the distribution of lag times experienced by patients included in each study within each meta-analysis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of the review.

claim: Real-world evidence, such as data from electronic medical or health records, can provide further insight into patient profiles, treatment choice, drug adherence, and adverse event management.
source: Finally, despite the importance of examining treatment variations among patients within clinical trial settings, which are circumscribed to well-established rules and procedures, real-world evidence, such as data from electronic medical or health records, can provide further insight into patient profiles, treatment choice, drug adherence, and adverse event management.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and draws from established knowledge about the value of real-world evidence.

claim: Individual-level factors not captured by the included meta-analyses can appreciably influence oncologic outcomes and thus the true causal effect of lag time on morbidity- and mortality-related outcomes.
source: These individual-level factors, which are not captured by the included meta-analyses, can appreciably influence oncologic outcomes and thus the true causal effect of lag time on morbidity- and mortality-related outcomes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on inference about limitations of the included studies.

claim: It can take years for cancer-related survival outcomes to accrue, making it too soon to accurately quantify the impact of extended times to diagnosis and treatment attributable to the pandemic.
source: As it can take years for cancer-related survival outcomes to accrue, it is too soon to accurately quantify the impact of extended times to diagnosis and treatment attributable to the pandemic.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and draws from established knowledge about cancer survival data accrual.

claim: The reported risk estimates represent the estimated associations between lag time and cancer outcomes prior to the pandemic, which can serve as a standard-of-care reference of these associations regardless of other changes to cancer care due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: The reported risk estimates therefore represent the estimated associations between lag time and cancer outcomes prior to the pandemic, which can serve as a standard-of-care reference of these associations regardless of other changes to cancer care due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on inference about the utility of the review findings.

claim: Direct comparison between risk estimates presented in this review cannot be made with risk estimates of the association between lag time and patient outcomes during the pandemic when made publicly available.
source: As such, direct comparison between risk estimates presented herein cannot be made with risk estimates of the association between lag time and patient outcomes during the pandemic when made publicly available.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on inference about the limitations of comparing pre- and post-pandemic data.

claim: The scoping review's tracing of defined lag times across relevant systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses can serve as a pre-pandemic reference when assessing the deviation in lag time duration attributable to the pandemic.
source: Instead, our tracing of defined lag times across relevant systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses can serve as a pre-pandemic reference when assessing the deviation in lag time duration attributable to the pandemic.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on inference about the utility of the review findings.

claim: Mapping the established relationships between lag time to care and oncologic outcomes when other elements of care were standard can help in constructing guidelines for flexible cancer care in the event of future public health emergencies.
source: Mapping the established relationships between lag time to care and oncologic outcomes when other elements of care were standard can help in constructing guidelines for flexible cancer care in the event of future public health emergencies.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on speculation about future applications of the review findings.

claim: The scoping review could lay the groundwork for observational and meta-analytical research on lag time intervals' influence on oncologic outcomes across sites beyond the most common ones, such as breast, lung, and colorectal.
source: Most importantly, this scoping review could lay the groundwork for observational and meta-analytical research on lag time intervals' influence on oncologic outcomes across sites beyond the most common ones, such as breast, lung, and colorectal.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on speculation about future research directions.

claim: The review's detailed exploration into the methodological gaps in lag time literature can assist in identifying key statistics to report such as the distribution of lag time duration experienced by patients, stratified estimates by treatment regimen, and adjustment for time-varying factors that altered during the pandemic.
source: Our detailed exploration into the methodological gaps in lag time literature can assist in identifying key statistics to report such as the distribution of lag time duration experienced by patients, stratified estimates by treatment regimen, and adjustment for time-varying factors that altered during the pandemic.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on inference about the utility of the review findings for future research.

claim: The lag time interval timeline emphasizes the granularity of exposure classification in cancer care.
source: Our lag time interval timeline, or mapping of lag times on the cancer care continuum, emphasizes the granularity of exposure classification in cancer care.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Conclusion section and is based on the visual representation in Figure 2.

claim: The lag time interval timeline can act as a blueprint for future studies assessing lag time intervals and/or multiple cancer sites.
source: This timeline can act as a blueprint for future studies assessing lag time intervals and/or multiple cancer sites.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Conclusion section and is based on speculation about future applications of the review findings.

claim: The extensive characterization of the effect of lag time on oncologic outcomes could aid in gauging lag times in cancer care experienced during the pandemic.
source: With regard to the COVID-19 pandemic, our extensive characterization of the effect of lag time on oncologic outcomes could aid in gauging lag times in cancer care experienced during the pandemic.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Conclusion section and is based on speculation about the utility of the review findings.
